{"id": "100:1/q08", "question": "What event is reported as the occasion of the opening?", "turns_on": "Which campaign or journey the narrations identify, and whether the debated Badr horse count bears on the verse's occasion.", "positions": [{"id": "100:1/q08/p1", "position": "A delayed expedition against Kinānah under al-Mundhir ibn ʿAmr was announced by the verses.", "reasons": "Muqātil says it went to Ḥunayn; others say against one or two Kinānah clans. Reports differ on whether Jews, hypocrites or both spread rumors that the men had died. Gabriel disclosed their route or success, reassuring the Prophet and worried relatives. Al-Qurṭubī identifies al-Mundhir as an al-ʿAqabah leader. Al-Wāḥidī glosses ashabat as ranging across broad plains. Ibn ʿĀshūr notes Ibn Kathīr found al-Bazzār's version very strange and the chain has weak Ḥafṣ b. Jamīʿ, though he thinks the story possible."}, {"id": "100:1/q08/p2", "position": "A delayed expedition to Tihāmah caused anxiety before Gabriel described its panting horses.", "reasons": "Muqātil's alternative says Jewish and hypocritical onlookers frightened those with missing relatives, and Gabriel came on Friday morning; the horses panted like foxes."}, {"id": "100:1/q08/p3", "position": "An unnamed cavalry detachment was away for a month without news.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAbbās says the Prophet sent cavalry; the missing news troubled him and the sūra described the horses' nostril-breathing, sparks, dawn assault, dust and entry into enemy ranks. Ibn Abī Ḥātim, al-Wāḥidī, Ibn al-Jawzī, al-Durr and al-Suyūṭī preserve versions. This account need not identify Badr. Al-Suyūṭī cites the month without news from Ibn ʿAbbās as an argument for Medinan revelation."}, {"id": "100:1/q08/p4", "position": "It followed ʿAlī's victory at Dhāt al-Salāsil.", "reasons": "An Abū ʿAbd Allāh report says earlier commanders returned, then ʿAlī prevailed. Another report says the Prophet recited the sūra at dawn after Gabriel announced victory; ʿAlī returned with prisoners and spoils. Dhāt al-Salāsil is explained by the captives being tied with rope-like chains; al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī cites Imams and some Sunni reports."}, {"id": "100:1/q08/p5", "position": "The horses or camels are linked to Badr.", "reasons": "Some commentators restrict Muslim horses to Badr, but ʿAlī's counterreport says it had only one or two horses, named variously as al-Miqdād's and al-Zubayr's. Other accounts use Badr as evidence for pilgrimage camels rather than an occasion of revelation. Al-Kashshāf reports ʿAlī challenging Ibn ʿAbbās's initial horse answer because Badr had only two horses; al-Ṭabarī's version says Ibn ʿAbbās retracted it."}]}
{"id": "100:1/q09", "question": "Was the sūra revealed in Mecca or Medina?", "turns_on": "Whether style favors early Mecca or the warhorse and expedition interpretation requires a Medinan setting.", "positions": [{"id": "100:1/q09/p1", "position": "Meccan.", "reasons": "Ibn Masʿūd, Jābir, al-Ḥasan, ʿIkrimah, ʿAṭāʾ and others are cited; Ibn Kathīr, al-Rāzī, al-Durr and Quṭb classify it so. Study Quran cites style and early Meccan placement. Elmalılı says this dating makes the later martial imagery a future allusion. Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī contests it because the images appear to concern jihad after the Hijra."}, {"id": "100:1/q09/p2", "position": "Medinan.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAbbās, Anas and Qatāda are cited. Al-Kalbī infers it if the oath is about warhorses, because permission to fight was in Medina. Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī adopts that inference; Ibn ʿĀshūr prefers this dating despite the weakness in the expedition report's chain. Ibn ʿĀshūr cautions that ʿAlī's camel statement itself does not specify either period. Al-Suyūṭī cites the month-long missing cavalry report as a Medinan argument, but says al-ʿĀdiyāt resembles Meccan revelation despite its Medinan classification."}]}
{"id": "100:1/q10", "question": "What is the sūra's verse count and revelation order?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "100:1/q10/p1", "position": "It has eleven verses; one Meccan ordering puts it fourteenth, after al-ʿAṣr and before al-Kawthar.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī, al-Durr, Quṭb and Ibn ʿĀshūr give eleven; Ibn ʿĀshūr cites Jābir b. Zayd's Meccan revelation order. Al-Māwardī separately notes that the following al-Qāriʿah is called Meccan by all authorities he cites."}]}
{"id": "100:1/q11", "question": "How is the sūra titled?", "turns_on": "Whether the sūra name includes the opening conjunction.", "positions": [{"id": "100:1/q11/p1", "position": "Al-ʿĀdiyāt, without the opening wāw.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr cites early Qayrawan, Tunisian and eastern codices and some commentaries. Biqāʿī says the title points to the purpose through the oath and its answer."}, {"id": "100:1/q11/p2", "position": "Wa-l-ʿĀdiyāt, retaining the initial wāw.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr says other tafsīrs preserve the opening wāw in the title."}]}
{"id": "100:1/q12", "question": "What recitation merit is reported for the sūra?", "turns_on": "The reports describe different reward measures.", "positions": [{"id": "100:1/q12/p1", "position": "It equals half the Qur'an in recitation reward.", "reasons": "Al-Ḥasan transmits a Prophetic saying assigning half to both al-Zalzalah and al-ʿĀdiyāt. A report through ʿAṭāʾ from Ibn ʿAbbās likewise assigns half to each, a third to al-Ikhlāṣ and a quarter to al-Kāfirūn."}, {"id": "100:1/q12/p2", "position": "Recitation brings ten good deeds for each person who spent the night at Muzdalifah and witnessed Jamʿ.", "reasons": "Jishumī and al-Kashshāf transmit the ten-deeds wording; al-Rāzī reports via Ubayy a reward measured by those who overnighted there and witnessed Jamʿ."}]}
{"id": "100:1/q13", "question": "What is said of the basmala before this sūra?", "turns_on": "The notes offer distinct spiritual and theological explanations of the basmala.", "positions": [{"id": "100:1/q13/p1", "position": "Its utterance, knowledge and love call for a guarded tongue, heart and spirit.", "reasons": "Al-Qushayrī calls it a jealous word: the tongue must avoid idle talk and backbiting, the heart be guarded, and the spirit be free of attachments and veils."}, {"id": "100:1/q13/p2", "position": "It presents God's sovereignty and His general and special mercy.", "reasons": "Biqāʿī says God commands all affairs, universally gives creation and clarification, and specially grants guidance and completed blessing to His devoted servants; the two notes repeat this account."}]}
{"id": "100:1/q14", "question": "Why swear by these chargers?", "turns_on": "Whether the oath chiefly honors valuable mounts, presents their obedience as evidence against people, honors the Prophet, or frames judgment.", "positions": [{"id": "100:1/q14/p1", "position": "To honor useful, noble mounts and call attention to God's gift.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī cites camels' many benefits in 88:17, God's service to people, and pilgrimage, invoking 3:97 against neglecting obligatory ḥajj; for horses he cites pursuit, retreat and religious uses and warns against display alone. His reading of 16:8 treats riding, not adornment, as the stated purpose. Biqāʿī says horses confer honor or wealth and receive reward or sin by use; good care in God's cause protects the owner, and their distinctive qualities ultimately point to the one sovereign giver. Ibn ʿĀshūr says pilgrims' service is esteemed by pagans and Muslims. Ibn al-Qayyim praises horses' strength and victory; Muḥammad ʿAbduh urges acquiring, training and riding them for defense. Islahi stresses clan protection, pedigree and their esteem in poetry, citing a Ḥamāsī poem. Kuran Yolu says horses were central to old warfare and beloved possessions through which God stresses the message."}, {"id": "100:1/q14/p2", "position": "The animals' dutiful exertion testifies against human ingratitude.", "reasons": "Islahi relates their exhausted obedience to 100:6 and rejects readings whose sanctity premise leaves the oath disconnected. Biqāʿī says the oath rebukes preference for transient wealth and failure to prepare for Judgment. Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī says human love of wealth and ingratitude are known to people and become evidence at judgment; Ibn ʿĀshūr says the sūra condemns these traits, warning even Muslims."}, {"id": "100:1/q14/p3", "position": "It is an oath by the Prophet's cavalry that honors him.", "reasons": "Ibn al-ʿArabī compares God's oath by Muḥammad in Yā Sīn and by his life in al-Ḥijr with the oath here by his cavalry, its neighing, dust and sparks."}, {"id": "100:1/q14/p4", "position": "It directs attention to coming judgment and the disclosure of deeds.", "reasons": "Biqāʿī reads the oath and answer as exposing the pursuit of status and wealth before the upheaval; Ibn ʿĀshūr says it promises reassurance to believers and threat to deniers. Study Quran divides the five charging verses, the ingratitude of 6–8 and the judgment of 9–11. Bint al-Shāṭiʾ says the familiar surprise of a dusty dawn raid prefigures the unseen Resurrection catching the ungrateful unprepared."}]}
{"id": "100:1/q15", "question": "How does the opening connect with the rest of the sūra and its neighbors?", "turns_on": "Different notes relate the opening to the moral claim, the closing resurrection, the preceding sūra, or a wider Qur'anic rhetorical pattern.", "positions": [{"id": "100:1/q15/p1", "position": "The raid's motion and sound anticipate ingratitude, graves opened and hearts exposed.", "reasons": "Quṭb likens the sūra's quick jumps and rough rumbling rhythm to the charging horse and to violent disclosure of graves and hearts; he says image and frame mirror one another. Bint al-Shāṭiʾ compares the familiar sudden dawn raid, dust and scattered targets with the unseen resurrection, people emerging in groups as in 99:6 and rapidly facing the All-Aware. Biqāʿī links the oath and answer to the sūra's purpose. Bint al-Shāṭiʾ compares the scattered targets of a dawn raid with people scattered from graves, citing 101:4 and 54:7 alongside 100:6 and 100:9–11."}, {"id"

: "100:1/q15/p2", "position": "After al-Zalzalah's judgment scene, this sūra shows the disposition behind evil deeds.", "reasons": "Biqāʿī says the prior sūra describes judgment, while this one traces the desire for worldly gain producing bad deeds. Study Quran reports an early Meccan ordering after al-Qāriʿah rather than this thematic link."}, {"id": "100:1/q15/p3", "position": "Its oath sequence creates a riddling rhetorical tension.", "reasons": "Corpus Coranicum compares the sequence with teaching questions at 90:12–16, 97:2–4, 101:1–11 and 104:5–9."}]}
{"id": "100:1/q16", "question": "What do the successive fāʾs imply?", "turns_on": "Whether the linkage simply orders the actions or also marks a causal relation at the sparks.", "positions": [{"id": "100:1/q16/p1", "position": "They mark the successive actions in one charge.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr calls this the normal pattern for successive adjectives or places, comparing Ibn Ziyābah's verse, while noting that 37:1 can use fāʾ for mention order. Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī says the sequence supports a particular raid; Elmalılı sees successive stages and even an age-by-age development of attack vehicles."}, {"id": "100:1/q16/p2", "position": "The first fāʾ also signals that the sparks result from hard running.", "reasons": "Bint al-Shāṭiʾ says the hooves strike stones as a consequence of the horses' pace."}]}
{"id": "100:1/q17", "question": "How is the verse read inwardly?", "turns_on": "The inward readings choose different spiritual processes for the charging image.", "positions": [{"id": "100:1/q17/p1", "position": "It depicts souls striving toward God and breathing out their longing.", "reasons": "Al-Qāshānī makes ascetic discipline and strenuous effort the runners, with panting the exhalation of longing. Al-Ālūsī describes yearning prayer, knowledge kindled by thought, and souls charging desire and habit toward sacred light. The allegory attributed to al-Bayḍāwī has souls convey holiness, kindle knowledge, attack caprice, raise desire and enter the highest Garden, with reference to 83:18–19."}, {"id": "100:1/q17/p2", "position": "It maps spiritual struggle through dhikr and the soul's passage from bodily darkness.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī's second account has remembrance kindle guidance in the body, the soul cross to dawn, stir passing thoughts and marshal the heart's forces in an army of remembrance."}]}
{"id": "100:1/q18", "question": "Are the opening oath passages classified as poetry or assigned a meter?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "100:1/q18/p1", "position": "Some classify the oath passages as poetry, and assign the opening of al-ʿĀdiyāt to al-basīṭ meter.", "reasons": "Al-Bāqillānī reports unnamed people calling passages from al-ʿĀdiyāt and al-Dhāriyāt poetry, with al-basīṭ assigned to the latter. Al-Zarkashī reports classification of both opening oath sequences as al-basīṭ."}]}
{"id": "100:1/q19", "question": "Is the tāʾ at the end of al-ʿādiyāt assimilated into the following ḍād?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "100:1/q19/p1", "position": "Ibn Khayrūn uniquely transmits Khallād's assimilation of the tāʾ into the following ḍād.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Jazarī reports this unique transmission from Ibn Khayrūn concerning Khallād's reading of wa-l-ʿādiyāti ḍabḥan."}]}
{"id": "100:6/q01", "question": "Who is 'the human' in this verse?", "turns_on": "Whether the generic definite describes the species' disposition, only some humans, unbelievers, or a named occasion.", "positions": [{"id": "100:6/q01/p1", "position": "Humankind generally is naturally prone to ingratitude, though divine protection, vigilance, and righteousness allow exceptions.", "reasons": "Biqaʿi treats rare sincere people as exceptions and links insān to familiarity with self and forgetfulness. Rāzī allows a general reading only as unprotected disposition. ʿIṣām al-Dīn prefers this reading because it praises warriors who overcome nature. Ibn ʿĀshūr grounds the tendency in self-preference, excepting prophets and the most righteous; Qurʾān 70:19, 21:37, 96:6–7 provide parallels. Elmalılı and Kuran Yolu report a broad human tendency."}, {"id": "100:6/q01/p2", "position": "The generic wording applies in judgment to some humans, especially the unguided, rather than every individual.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī distinguishes generic wording from the limited class judged. Elmalılı allows some members. Kuran Yolu attributes a focus on those without guidance to Rāzī."}, {"id": "100:6/q01/p3", "position": "The human is the unbeliever or a particular unbeliever.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAbbās reads the generic word as the unbeliever; al-Qurṭubī likens him to sterile earth. Rāzī argues that the mention of raised graves in 100:9 suits denial of resurrection; al-Wāḥidī calls the human an unbeliever."}, {"id": "100:6/q01/p4", "position": "The verse concerns Qurṭ or Qurāẓ ibn ʿAbd Allāh.", "reasons": "Muqātil says he ate alone, starved his servant, and gave nothing to his people; names vary as Qurṭ, Qurāẓ, and Qurṭah, with differing patronymics. Rāzī cites Ibn ʿAbbās for the occasion and the resurrection context. Al-Ālūsī questions both the identification and the argument."}, {"id": "100:6/q01/p5", "position": "The verse concerns al-Walīd ibn al-Mughīra.", "reasons": "Al-Ḍaḥḥāk transmits this occasion; Ibn ʿĀshūr reports it as a proposed identification."}, {"id": "100:6/q01/p6", "position": "The raided people are the ungrateful ones, since they rejected Islam.", "reasons": "Ṭabāṭabāʾī calls Islam God's greatest blessing, bringing good life and eternal happiness."}]}
{"id": "100:6/q02", "question": "What does 'his Lord' emphasize about the one wronged?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "100:6/q02/p1", "position": "He is the benefactor who created, preserves, sustains, governs, and nurtures humanity, making ingratitude especially grave.", "reasons": "Biqaʿi lists God's care; al-Zamakhsharī compares even the greatest human gift, parents, with God's smallest favor and says human benefaction is more immediately visible. Ibn ʿĀshūr says the object is the one most deserving thanks."}]}
{"id": "100:6/q03", "question": "How does 'to his Lord' attach grammatically?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "100:6/q03/p1", "position": "It attaches to kanūd as its object, with lām marking the relation despite the intervening emphatic lām.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr says the derived adjective is not inherently transitive and regularly takes an object with lām; Ibn Hishām says the predicate lām need not occupy initial position. Al-Ālūsī likewise attaches the phrase to the predicate."}]}
{"id": "100:6/q04", "question": "Why is 'to his Lord' put before kanūd?", "turns_on": "The sources offer compatible or alternative motives: verse ending, special blame, or restriction.", "positions": [{"id": "100:6/q04/p1", "position": "Its placement preserves the verse ending or rhyme.", "reasons": "Al-Samīn and al-Ālūsī explicitly cite the line ending; Bursevī says it also fits the rhyme."}, {"id": "100:6/q04/p2", "position": "Its placement spotlights the enormity of ingratitude toward God.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī calls ingratitude for God's favor especially blameworthy; Ibn ʿĀshūr says God is the one most deserving thanks and the predicate lām adds astonished emphasis."}, {"id": "100:6/q04/p3", "position": "Its placement provides emphasis or restrictive focus.", "reasons": "Bursevī allows emphasis or restriction; al-Ālūsī reports emphatic restriction."}]}
{"id": "100:6/q05", "question": "What does kanūd mean or describe here?", "turns_on": "Whether the word's core is denial of blessings, withholding good, disobedience, or a particular conduct; regional usage and poetic evidence account for many glosses.", "positions": [{"id": "100:6/q05/p1", "position": "One who is intensely ungrateful, denying or failing to thank for blessings.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAbbās, Mujāhid, Qatāda, al-Ḥasan, al-Rabīʿ and many others transmit the gloss; Ibn Zayd cites 22:66. Al-Ṭabarī, Abū ʿUbayda, Ibn Qutayba, al-Wāḥidī and Bint al-Shāṭiʾ compare barren land that produces nothing. Al-Aʿshā and anonymous poets apply it to failure to return another's favor. Dialect reports put this sense in Muḍar, Rabīʿa, Quḍāʿa, Kināna or, in al-Farrāʾ and Bint al-Shāṭiʾ, Kinda and Ḥaḍramawt. Al-Qurṭubī and al-Ālūsī say other traits return to this sense; Bint al-Shāṭiʾ prefers it in context."}, {"id": "100:6/q05/p2", "position": "One who complains to God, counts misfortunes, and forgets blessings.", "reasons": "Al-Ḥasan's repeated explanation is supported by complaint poetry; Rāzī compares 89:16. Al-Fuḍayl says a single offense erases many favors from memory; Biqaʿi emphasizes the small hardship against abundant blessing."}, {"id": "100:6/q05/p3", "position": "One who eats or lives alone, withholds food or support, and beats or starves a servant.", "reasons": "A report from Abū Umāma attributes the three acts to the Prophet; a separate Ibn ʿAbbās report calls such a person among the worst. Ibn Kathīr and al-Suyūṭī call the marfūʿ chain weak because Jaʿfar ibn al-Zubayr is abandoned; al-Ṭabarī and al-Ālūsī preserve a mawqūf Abū Umāma route. Qatāda and al-Ḥasan say the listed traits must occur together. Al-Qurṭubī gives the Prophetic gloss priority if sound; Ibn ʿĀshūr treats the acts as lesser degrees of ingratitude."}, {"id": "100:6/q05/p4", "position": "One who withholds due rights, gifts, or help, including aid to his community in calamity.", "reasons": "Al-Wāḥidī and al-Mubarrad make withholding a due right the root sense, comparing barren ground; ʿAṭāʾ specifies failure to aid one's people. Al-Aʿshā's visitor poetry and Abū Zubayd's withheld connection illustrate the usage."}, {"id": "100:6/q05/p5", "position": "A miser or stingy person.", "reasons": "Regional accounts give Banū Mālik or Kināna as the tribe and sometimes add poor treatment of dependents. Abū Zubayd and Ibrāhīm ibn Harmah supply poetry; Ibn Qutayba's barren ground and Study Quran's petty person offer analogies."},

{"id": "100:6/q05/p6", "position": "A disobedient, rebellious, or sinning person.", "reasons": "Many dialect reports assign this sense to Kinda and Ḥaḍramawt, while al-Farrāʾ and Bint al-Shāṭiʾ transmit an ungrateful sense for those same dialects; some omit Ḥaḍramawt. Al-Zajjāj glosses the person as a disbeliever."}, {"id": "100:6/q05/p7", "position": "One who denies the truth or disbelieves.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAbbās and Mujāhid say kāfūr; al-Māwardī reports truth-denial as a distinct gloss. The etymology connecting Kinda with severing or rejecting its father is cited by al-Ṭabarī, al-Zamakhsharī, Rāzī and al-Qurṭubī."}, {"id": "100:6/q05/p8", "position": "One who cuts the bond of thanks or connection.", "reasons": "Al-Qurṭubī derives the word from cutting a rope, citing al-Aʿshā's cutting poem; the Kinda name is also explained as cutting off one's father. Al-Ṭabarī and al-Aʿshā use severed customary affection as lexical evidence."}, {"id": "100:6/q05/p9", "position": "One with little good, like land that bears no crop.", "reasons": "Abū ʿUbayda gives the gloss; several lexicographers explain barren earth as kanūd. Bursevī suggests a reversal of nakd; Ibn ʿAbbās compares the unbeliever to barren earth."}, {"id": "100:6/q05/p10", "position": "One who spends God's gifts in disobedience.", "reasons": "Al-Māwardī, al-Wāsiṭī and Biqāʿī identify misuse of the very gifts God supplied; Biqāʿī names horses and mental and bodily strength. Ibn ʿĀshūr calls this one degree among shirk and disobedience."}, {"id": "100:6/q05/p11", "position": "One who credits blessings to himself or his helpers, overlooking their Giver.", "reasons": "Al-Warrāq supplies the attribution; al-Tirmidhī and Dhū al-Nūn say such a person sees the gift but not God. Al-Qāshānī says the gifts veil a person from reaching Him; Sūlamī says he sees what comes from himself, not what comes to him."}, {"id": "100:6/q05/p12", "position": "One heedless even while resting amid blessing.", "reasons": "Al-Sulamī and al-Qushayrī describe his head on the cushion of blessing while the heart remains heedless."}, {"id": "100:6/q05/p13", "position": "One resentful, envious, or ignorant of his own worth.", "reasons": "Al-Qurṭubī reports the variants and a maxim that failure to know one's worth exposes one's veil; he subsumes them under ingratitude."}, {"id": "100:6/q05/p14", "position": "One who breaks covenant and abandons truth through attachment to passion.", "reasons": "Al-Tustarī says habitual passion leads God to make such a person despair of goodness and piety."}, {"id": "100:6/q05/p15", "position": "One who rejects small favors and fails to thank for great ones.", "reasons": "Al-Māwardī and al-Qurṭubī transmit this distinction; Biqāʿī relates it to the intensive form."}]}
{"id": "100:6/q06", "question": "What other creature can kanūd describe in Arabic usage?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "100:6/q06/p1", "position": "A horse.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyyah reports this usage and cites Abū Zubayd's poetry as evidence."}]}
{"id": "100:6/q07", "question": "What does the form kanūd convey?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "100:6/q07/p1", "position": "It is an intensive adjective conveying deep or habitual ingratitude.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr explicitly calls it intensive; Biqāʿī and Elmalılı link the form to scorn for small favors and loss of gratitude after hardship. Al-Qurṭubī notes kanūd as masculine and kanūd or kand for a woman."}]}
{"id": "100:6/q08", "question": "What is the response to the preceding oath?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "100:6/q08/p1", "position": "The assertion beginning 'Indeed, the human...' is its response.", "reasons": "Qushayrī, al-Wāḥidī, Ibn ʿAṭiyya, al-Bayḍāwī and others identify verse 6 as the oath's answer. Rāzī calls it the first of three assertions. Al-Samīn says 'to his Lord' is fronted for the endings. Ibn ʿĀshūr names verses 1–5 as the oath."}]}
{"id": "100:6/q09", "question": "How does the horse oath support the accusation of ingratitude?", "turns_on": "The oath can contrast noble animal service with human conduct, portray acquisitive raiding, or act as evidence through horses' obedience.", "positions": [{"id": "100:6/q09/p1", "position": "Noble horses and fighters contrast with the ungrateful human.", "reasons": "Biqāʿī compares charging horses to galloping human thoughts, which can serve truth or falsehood; he says raiding often seeks unjust goods and even jihad may lack sincerity, citing a qudsī report about remembering God in combat. Bursevī sees either known expedition horses or all horses in God's cause and says fighters have still greater merit. Asad's classical commentators treat believing chargers as laudable."}, {"id": "100:6/q09/p2", "position": "Horses' obedient service to humans exposes humans' failure to serve God.", "reasons": "Iṣlāḥī says animals know their master's rights, whereas humans benefit from horses yet ignore God. He cites warhorses' clan value and Ḥamāsī poetry, extends the example to camels, and says God subjected animals to people. He rejects the warrior-horse interpretation as leaving the oath unrelated to verse 6."}, {"id": "100:6/q09/p3", "position": "Charging horses symbolize appetites through which people forget God and responsibility.", "reasons": "Asad links the charge to surrender to appetites and cites 14:48 and 20:105–107 for the judgment setting."}, {"id": "100:6/q09/p4", "position": "The oath by horses provides evidence that humans are ungrateful.", "reasons": "Iṣlāḥī states the evidentiary role explicitly; Biqāʿī says the oath rebukes neglect of judgment and thanklessness."}]}

{"id": "101:6/q03", "question": "What makes these balances heavy?", "turns_on": "Whether weight describes predominating good deeds, adherence to truth, intrinsic worth and approval, divine determination, or inward perfections.", "positions": [{"id": "101:6/q03/p1", "position": "The person's good deeds outweigh evil deeds or otherwise prevail.", "reasons": "Muqatil, al-Tabari, al-Wahidi, al-Baghawi, al-Zamakhshari, al-Baydawi, Ibn Kathir, Elmalili, Islahi, and Study Quran explain the weight as prevailing good. {"id": "101:7/q03", "question": "What does rāḍiya mean, and how can life bear this description?", "turns_on": "The participle can be parsed as possessive, figuratively passive or transferred, literally active of the life, or as a concealed metaphor; feminine marking is an objection to the possessive parse.", "positions": [{"id": "101:7/q03/p1", "position": "It is a relational or possessive adjective: a life endowed with satisfaction.", "reasons": "Naḥḥās, al-Zajjāj as cited by Baghawī and Rāzī, and al-Khalīl and Sībawayh as cited by Ibn ʿAṭiyya treat it as a possessive construction. ITQAN says an active participle can carry a passive sense, comparing this pleasing or pleased-with life to water described as poured forth."}, {"id": "101:7/q03/p3", "position": "The life itself is pleased with its inhabitants and remains with them.", "reasons": "Al-Sīrāfī offers this as an active sense of the adjective, accounting for its feminine ending; Elmalılı repeats that the life stays attached to its people."}, {"id": "101:7/q03/p4", "position": "The life itself actively satisfies its inhabitants by yielding gently to their wishes.", "reasons": "Qurṭubī says its softness and submission give the life an active role; the couches, fruit branches and rivers in Paradise illustrate its generous compliance."}, {"id": "101:7/q03/p5", "position": "It is a concealed metaphor with an imaginative metaphorical feature.", "reasons": "Ālūsī and Elmalılı report this analysis from works of rhetoric without supplying a more specific image."}]}
